ol96b1-d1e205.summary: Part 1 of the prologue joins a festive, sermon-style commendation of Lombard's Sentences to Auriol's first question on the epistemic status of theology. The praeambulum, on Ezekiel's 'book written within and without', presents the Sentences as Scripture unrolled: useful, easy and full of worth, serving instruction, faith, refutation of heretics, the advanced and the weak, and mapping the four books onto God's mysteries, creation, precepts and judgment. The question then asks what habit theological study acquires. Auriol rejects Thomas's subalternation to the science of the blessed (the articles are conclusions theology argues toward, and believed principles cannot ground science), Ware's 'science in itself', the 'science of consequences', Godfrey's science of Scripture's content, and Scotus's three habits (certainty cannot be separated from evidence). He distinguishes metaphysical demonstration, explicated faith and opinion, and concludes that properly theological study yields a distinct habit that causes no assent, is purely declarative, and is wisdom in the sense of understanding. Faith gives adherence and theology clarity.
claims: The Sentences unfold and make accessible the obscure content of Scripture.
Theological study acquires a habit distinct from faith.
The articles of faith are conclusions theology declares and defends, not its principles.
Theology is not a subalternate science, a science of consequences, or knowledge of Scripture's text.
The theological habit causes no assent; it is purely declarative and is wisdom.
Faith supplies adherence and theology clarity.

ol96b1-d1e220.summary: Part 2 of the prologue expounds the opening of Lombard's prologue and asks, prompted by Lombard's trust in divine help, whether God can give a wayfarer a light by which the articles are known scientifically. The praeambulum divides the Sentences into prologue, treatise and epilogue and gives Lombard's three motives: trust in divine reward, zeal against error, and love of students. The question rejects Henry of Ghent's intermediate light, since no light can show the articles' truth under the common concepts wayfarers have, the connection of terms being knowable only through proper concepts. It defends against Hervaeus Scotus's claim that abstractive cognition can concern existence, then corrects Scotus with Auriol's celebrated theory of intuitive cognition. From experience (afterimages, dreams, illusions) and from divine power, intuition can occur without its object's presence or existence; intuitive and abstractive (quasi-imaginative) cognition differ in mode, as presential versus absent appearance, not in object. Auriol concludes that both modes are possible in the intellect and regarding God, that only intuitive cognition of God is beatific, and that a quasi-imaginative cognition of the deity could be given to a wayfarer and would yield propter quid science of the articles.
claims: Lombard wrote the Sentences from trust in God, zeal against error, and love of students.
No light can show the articles' truth under the common concepts wayfarers have.
Intuitive cognition can occur without the presence or existence of its object.
Intuitive and imaginative cognition differ in mode of appearance, not object.
Only intuitive cognition of God is beatific.
God could give a wayfarer quasi-imaginative cognition of the deity, yielding scientific knowledge of the articles.

ol96b1-d1e224.summary: Part 3 of the prologue expounds Lombard's answer to critics and heretics and asks whether theology is practical or speculative, prompted by Lombard's aim to refute heretics and defend faith. The praeambulum traces heresy to envy, self-will, neglect of study and vainglory, sealed by obstinacy, and presents the Sentences as a weapon of testimonies against it. The question reviews twelve opinions, rejecting the purely speculative views, Ware's supernatural prudence, Scotus's restriction of praxis to the will, Godfrey's two habits, Thomas's 'simply speculative, qualifiedly practical', and the affective views of Giles of Rome and John of Paris. Against Scotus it reworks the notion of the practical: praxis can be intellectual (logic and rhetoric are practical), practicality consists formally in activity toward an object operable by the knower, and speculative and practical essentially divide science as an intellectual virtue. Auriol concludes that theology is purely practical, directing belief immediately and love ultimately; that it resides in the speculative intellect; and that it is nobler than any speculative science.
claims: Heresy springs from moral failings and is sealed by obstinacy; the Sentences aim to refute it.
Theology is a purely practical habit directing faith and charity.
A habit is practical formally by its activity toward an object operable by the knower.
Logic and rhetoric are practical habits.
Theology resides in the speculative intellect yet is practical.
Theology is nobler than any speculative science.

ol96b1-d1e230.summary: Part 4 of the prologue expounds Lombard's statement of his book's authority (woven from the Fathers), utility (a compact anthology) and his humility, and asks whether the theological habit is one or many, prompted by the unity of Lombard's single volume. Auriol first analyzes the scientific habit. Against Henry (one indivisible quality intensified), Scotus (an aggregate of complete partial habits) and Bernard of Auvergne (an order of species), science is a permanent habit by which the intellect grasps a conclusion through its principle in one simple act, distinct from remembered demonstrations. A science is numerically one as a whole of mutually perfecting partial habits, connected along and across chains of demonstration. After rejecting accounts of theology's unity by revealability (Thomas), authority, middle, formal object (Scotus), their concurrence, and Godfrey's two habits, he holds that a science is specifically one by a single mode of knowing and proper logic. Theology is therefore one habit, defined by declaratively using whatever supports faith, with God and creatures falling under it by attribution.
claims: The Sentences derive their authority from the Fathers and are useful as a compact anthology.
Science is a permanent habit grasping conclusions through principles in one simple act.
A science is numerically one as a connected whole of partial habits.
A science is specifically one by a single mode of knowing and proper logic.
Theology is one habit, numerically and specifically.

ol96b1-d1e235.summary: Part 5 of the prologue expounds Lombard's prefixing of chapter titles and asks whether theology's subject is God under the formality of deity, prompted by Lombard's division of his work. Auriol rejects Scotus's definition of a subject as what first virtually contains all of a science's truths. Explicitly following Aristotle and Averroes against modern novelties, he defines a subject as a genus fixing one mode of abstraction, classifying twelve human sciences by the intellect's reflexive, extended or purely abstract stances. He rejects Christ, things and signs (Bonaventure), the revealable (Thomas), divine being, God as glorifier (Giles), as end (Thomas of Strasbourg) or as unknown, and Scotus's 'infinite being' as the wayfarer's subject. He concludes that deity is theology's subjective character, mediating all its predications and explaining its declarative mode, reached by the wayfarer through a proper but analogical concept prior to 'infinite being'. Theology's six-part division corresponds to the books of the Sentences, and it is broader than metaphysics and regulates philosophy. An appended article identifies bodily substance (not mobile being) as natural philosophy's subject and speech expressive of concepts as logic's.
claims: Lombard prefixed chapter titles for readers' convenience.
A science's subject is a genus fixing one mode of abstraction; virtual containment is not its mark.
God under the formality of deity is theology's subject.
The wayfarer has a proper, analogical concept of deity prior to 'infinite being'.
Theology's six considerations correspond to the structure of the Sentences.
Bodily substance is natural philosophy's subject; speech expressive of concepts is logic's.

ol96b1-d1e201.summary: The prologue to Auriol's commentary on book 1 combines a running literal exposition of Lombard's prologue with five questions forming a systematic theory of theology as a discipline. A sermon commends the Sentences as Scripture unrolled, and the expositions follow Lombard's motives, his answer to critics and heretics, the book's authority and utility, and his chapter titles. The questions then build a coherent position. (1) Theological study yields a habit distinct from faith that causes no assent but is purely declarative and is wisdom; the articles are conclusions it declares, not principles from which it argues. (2) No light can make the articles scientifically evident under wayfarers' common concepts, though a quasi-imaginative cognition of the deity could; along the way Auriol gives his famous theory that intuitive cognition can exist without its object, intuitive and imaginative cognition differing by mode of appearance. (3) Theology is purely practical, directing faith and charity, since practicality consists in activity toward an operable object, and it resides in the speculative intellect. (4) Theology is one habit, since a science is numerically one as a connected whole and specifically one by its mode of knowing. (5) Its subject is God under the formality of deity, reached through an analogical concept, with sciences in general distinguished by modes of abstraction. Throughout Auriol argues against Thomas, Scotus, Henry of Ghent, Godfrey of Fontaines and others, appealing to Aristotle and Averroes.
claims: Theology is a declarative habit distinct from faith, adding clarity but not assent.
The articles of faith are conclusions theology declares, not its principles.
Intuitive cognition can occur without the existence of its object.
No light can make the articles evident under the wayfarer's common concepts.
Theology is purely practical, directing faith and charity.
Theology is one habit by its single declarative mode of knowing.
God under the formality of deity is theology's subject, conceived analogically by the wayfarer.

ol96b1-d1e2173.summary: Distinction 37 concerns how God is in things. The literal exposition follows Lombard: God is in all things by essence, presence and power and in the saints by grace; he is wholly everywhere by essence, not only by power, without defilement or change; and created spirits are in place definitively, not circumscriptively. The question asks whether God is everywhere by essence, presence and power. Rejecting presence as operation (Thomas), as a real relation separable from operation with action at a distance (Scotus), as infinite spiritual magnitude (Richard of Middleton), as an order of coexistence (Durand), and as simultaneity, Auriol holds that God is everywhere by complete non-distance (indistantia). This is a negative condition without nearness or positional relation, determined by operation, since no power can be distant from its operation, and so it belongs only to God, who acts everywhere. Operation thus demonstrates non-distance though not positive presence; no created power acts at a distance (the sun's causality runs through alteration that educes forms from matter); and given the faith-held premise of universal conservation, omnipresence is demonstrable on supposition. Essence, presence and power are substrate, formal character and determinant of one mode. Immensity is deity connoting necessary non-absence from every possible place, all things are in God because of their dependence, presence by grace is the same mode singularized by grace's intense operation, and God's presence in Christ follows from the hypostatic union.
claims: God is in all things by essence, presence and power, and in the saints by grace.
God is everywhere by complete non-distance, not by positive presence, simultaneity, order or magnitude.
No power acts immediately at a distance; operation proves its power's non-distance.
Given universal conservation, omnipresence is demonstrable on supposition.
Essence, presence and power are three aspects of one mode of omnipresence.
Presence by grace is the same mode intensified; presence in Christ follows from the hypostatic union.
God becomes present to new creatures without change.

ol96b1.summary: Partial summary of Peter Auriol's Scriptum on book 1 of the Sentences, resting only on the prologue and distinction 37. The other 47 direct divisions (distinctions 1 to 36 and 38 to 48) have no interpretations yet, so this is not a summary of the whole work. In these two parts Auriol appears as an independent, polemical commentator who engages Thomas, Scotus, Henry of Ghent, Godfrey of Fontaines, Durand and others at length and appeals to Aristotle and Averroes. The prologue sets out a theory of theology: an acquired, purely declarative habit distinct from faith and identified with wisdom, purely practical in directing faith and charity, one by its single mode of knowing, with God under the formality of deity as subject, conceived analogically by wayfarers. Along the way come his theory of intuitive cognition without an existing object and a classification of the sciences by modes of abstraction. Distinction 37 explains God's omnipresence as complete non-distance determined by operation rather than any positive presence, and derives from it accounts of immensity, presence by grace, and God's presence in Christ.
claims: (Partial, prologue) Theology is a declarative, practical habit distinct from faith, with God as deity as its subject.
(Partial, prologue) Intuitive cognition can occur without its object.
(Partial, d. 37) God is everywhere by complete non-distance determined by his operation.
